title: 5.8.13 Lab: Reap the dead with filter
description: Dead enemies stay in the array, so the list never shortens and the next hit lands on a corpse. Build a new list of the living with `filter` and store it back in `enemies`.

steps.title: Keep only the living
steps.instructions:
`filter` builds a new array from the ones that pass a test; it does not change the old array. Use it to keep the enemies where `isAlive()` is true, and store the result back in `enemies`. Put it after the hit check and before the loop.

Press Space six times. Every enemy starts with 4 hp and each hit takes 2, so it takes two presses to finish one: the counter at the bottom should go 3 → 2 → 1 → 0, dropping on every second press, and each press should hit a living enemy.
hints: The shape is in 3.7.20 (Worked Example: Chaining `.map()` off a `.push()`-Built Array): `curved.filter((score) => score >= 80)` keeps the scores that pass the test. Here that is `enemies = enemies.filter((e) => e.isAlive());`.
`filter` hands back a new array, so writing `enemies.filter(...)` without `enemies =` throws the result away.

requirements.title: A filtered list is stored back in enemies
requirements.description: `filter` is used and its result is assigned back to `enemies`, so the array itself gets shorter (a new list filled with push in a loop and stored back in `enemies`, or a loop that splices out the dead, also counts). Help: 3.7.20 (Worked Example: Chaining `.map()` off a `.push()`-Built Array)

requirements.title: The test keeps the enemies that are still alive
requirements.description: The filter keeps the living — it asks each enemy `isAlive()`, or compares its health (a loop that pushes the living into a new list, or splices out the enemies that are not alive, also counts). Help: 3.7.20 (Worked Example: Chaining `.map()` off a `.push()`-Built Array)

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote a moSHion sketch (p5-style JavaScript with a physics world) for the lab "5.8.13 Lab: Reap the dead with filter". The task they were given: Dead enemies stay in the enemies array, so the list never gets shorter and Space keeps hitting a corpse at the front. After the hit check and before the loop in draw(), build a new list that keeps only the enemies that are still alive, using filter, and store it back in enemies, so the count at the bottom goes 3, 2, 1, 0. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do when the sketch runs. moSHion facts that matter here: setup() runs once; draw() runs about 60 times a second, and so does every function it calls. kb.presses('space') is true only on the one frame a key goes down; kb.pressing('space') is true on every frame it is held. y grows downward. Each enemy has isAlive(), true while its hp is above 0. filter builds a NEW array of the items whose test is true and does not change the old one, so its result has to be stored back in enemies or it is thrown away. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable, parameter and helper-function names, template strings, arrow functions, a ternary or an if/else chain, x++ or x += 1 or x = x + 1, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Names that other code in the program already calls (isAlive) must keep those names, because a renamed one is never called. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment or a string never runs, and the STEP comments the starter came with are not the student's work. These other ways of rebuilding the list also work and count as met on both criteria; say in the note that filter is the tool this lab practises: a new empty list filled with push in a loop over enemies (for...of, a counting loop or forEach) that pushes only the living and is then stored back in enemies; a loop that walks enemies from the end to the start and splices out each enemy that is not alive; a while loop that splices or shifts out the enemies that are not alive; a loop from the start that splices out a dead enemy and then steps its counter back (i--). Write each note for THIS student's own code, for a 14-year-old reader: short sentences, plain words. In a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.

rubric.title: A filtered list is stored back in enemies
rubric.description: Every frame, filter runs on enemies and its result ends up in enemies again (enemies = enemies.filter(...), or kept in another variable first and then assigned to enemies). Also met, with a note that filter is the tool this lab practises: a new list filled with push in a loop over enemies and then stored back in enemies; a loop from the end that splices out each dead enemy; a while loop that splices or shifts out the dead; a loop from the start that splices and then steps its counter back (i--). Calling enemies.filter(...) without storing the result is not met: nothing changes.

rubric.title: The test keeps the enemies that are still alive
rubric.description: The test inside filter keeps the living, in any shape: it asks each enemy isAlive(), or keeps those whose hp is above 0 (an arrow with or without braces, a function with return, === true). In a loop that pushes into a new list, the push must happen only for the enemies that ARE alive; in a loop that splices or shifts, it must happen for the enemies that are NOT alive. A test that keeps the dead (such as !e.isAlive() inside filter, or hp <= 0) is the opposite and not met.
